title: How to Put Ribbon on a Christmas Tree (7 Mistakes That Look CHEAP)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, I can walk into any house in December and tell if the tree was done by a decorator or by a tired family at eleven o'clock at night. It's not the ornaments. It's the ribbon and the top. A decorator's tree has ribbon that tumbles down like a waterfall, and a topper that looks like it belongs. A tired tree has a ribbon wrapped like a mummy and a star leaning sideways.
scenes.caption: LIKE A WATERFALL

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you seven ribbon and tree topper mistakes that make a tree look cheap, and the easy fixes, so yours looks like it came out of a department store window. And stay with me, because the last one is the trick for keeping the topper straight, and it uses something you already have in your kitchen drawer.
scenes.caption: SEVEN MISTAKES

scenes.text: When I was a girl, my mother took me to Cleveland every December to see the Christmas windows at the big department stores downtown. Halle Brothers and Higbee's. There was a tree in one window, in nineteen fifty-three, with wide red velvet ribbon tumbling down from the top in long streams, and a gold star that almost touched the ceiling. I stood there so long my feet went numb in the snow.
scenes.caption: MY FEET WENT NUMB

scenes.text: On the bus home, my mother asked me what I liked best. I said the ribbon. The next year, she bought two yards of red ribbon at the five and dime, and we tried to make our little tree look like Halle's. It didn't, honey. But we kept trying, every year, and by the time I was twenty, we'd figured out every secret. In a minute I'll show you the first one.
scenes.caption: WE KEPT TRYING

scenes.text: Mistake number one. Wrapping the ribbon around the tree in a spiral, round and round, tight against the branches, like a bandage. It flattens the tree and looks like a candy cane stripe. The decorator's way is vertical. Start at the top, and let the ribbon fall down the tree in long, loose streams, from the top to the bottom, like water running down a hill.
scenes.caption: LIKE A BANDAGE

scenes.text: Here's how. Cut the ribbon into lengths, each one the height of the tree. Tuck one end into the branches near the top. Then let it fall down, tucking it into the tree every foot or so, pushing it in deep so it disappears, then letting it puff out again. In, out, in, out, like a gentle wave. Do five or six streams, evenly spaced around the tree.
scenes.caption: IN, OUT, IN, OUT

scenes.text: Mistake number two. Ribbon that's too skinny. A thin little ribbon, an inch wide, disappears into the tree. You can't even see it from across the room. For a tree, you want wide ribbon, two and a half inches at least, and four inches for a big tree. And wired ribbon, with thin wire sewn into the edges, so you can bend it and shape it, and it holds those pretty waves.
scenes.caption: WIRED AND WIDE

scenes.text: How much? For a seven-foot tree, plan on about three or four rolls of ten yards each. It sounds like a lot, honey. But skimping on ribbon is like putting half a frosting on a cake. And buy it the day after Christmas, at half price, for next year. That's the only way I ever bought ribbon in my life.
scenes.caption: HALF A FROSTING

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Too many kinds of ribbon. Red plaid, gold glitter, silver mesh, and polka dots, all on one tree. It looks like a craft store exploded. Pick one ribbon, or two that go together. A red velvet and a gold, or a plaid with a matching solid. Then repeat them all around the tree. Repetition is what makes it look planned.
scenes.caption: A CRAFT STORE EXPLODED

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And a little trick. If you use two ribbons, lay them on top of each other, the wide one underneath and the narrow one on top, and treat them as one. It looks rich and layered, and it's no more work. My mother did a red velvet with a thin gold ribbon on top, and it looked like a king's robe.
scenes.caption: LIKE A KING'S ROBE

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Putting the ribbon on last, after all the ornaments. Then it sits on top of everything and squashes the ornaments. The right order is lights first, then the ribbon, then the big ornaments, then the small ones. The ribbon goes on before the ornaments, so they can hang in front of it and around it, and everything looks woven together.
scenes.caption: LIGHTS, RIBBON, ORNAMENTS

scenes.text: So far, ribbon falling down, not wrapped round. Wide and wired. One or two kinds, repeated. And the ribbon before the ornaments. Now, the tree topper. And here's mistake number five. A topper that's too small for the tree. A little four-inch star on a seven-foot tree looks like a lost button. The topper should be about a tenth of the height of the tree.
scenes.caption: A LOST BUTTON

scenes.text: So for a seven-foot tree, a topper about eight or nine inches tall, or bigger. A star, an angel, a big bow, or a spray of branches and picks. And it doesn't have to be fancy. My mother's angel was made from a paper doily, a wooden bead for a head, and a pipe cleaner halo. I made it in second grade, in nineteen fifty-one, and it went on top of her tree for forty years.
scenes.caption: A PAPER DOILY ANGEL

scenes.text: And here's a decorator's trick for a topper that looks grand. Make a big bow from your tree ribbon, with long tails, and put it at the very top. Then let the tails fall down the tree, and they become the first streams of ribbon. Then tuck a few tall sprays of glittery picks or dried branches behind the bow, sticking up and out. It looks like a firework at the top.
scenes.caption: LIKE A FIREWORK

scenes.text: Mistake number six. A bare, skinny top of the tree, with a topper stuck on a single stick, all alone. Most trees get thin at the top. The fix is to fill in the space just under the topper. Put your biggest, shiniest ornaments up there, cluster a few sprays of picks or ribbon loops around it, and add a few extra lights. Then the topper sits in a nest instead of on a pole.
scenes.caption: A NEST, NOT A POLE

scenes.text: And now mistake number seven, the trick I promised. The leaning topper. Every year, it starts straight, and by Christmas morning it's tipped over, like it had too much eggnog. Here's the fix from your kitchen drawer. A wooden spoon, or a paint stirrer, or a chopstick. Tie it to the top of the trunk with a few twist ties or zip ties, so it sticks up straight and strong.
scenes.caption: FROM YOUR KITCHEN DRAWER

scenes.text: Then slide the topper over it, or tie the topper to it with floral wire. The wooden spoon gives the skinny treetop a backbone. Your star or angel will stand straight until the sixth of January. My father figured that out in nineteen fifty-six. Before that, our angel spent every Christmas looking at the floor like she'd lost a contact lens.
scenes.caption: A BACKBONE

scenes.text: And put the topper on first, sweetheart, not last. Do it right after the lights, while you can still reach the top without knocking off a dozen ornaments. Stand on a sturdy step stool, not a chair, and have somebody hold it. And turn the lights on before you start decorating, so you can see where the dark spots are.
scenes.caption: THE TOPPER GOES ON FIRST

scenes.text: When you're finished, step back across the room, and squint your eyes. It sounds silly, but it works. When you squint, you see the shapes and the light instead of the details. If one side looks empty, or a ribbon stream is crooked, or there's a dark hole, you'll see it right away. My mother squinted at our tree every year, and my father said she looked like a sea captain.
scenes.query: woman stepping back looking at tree
scenes.caption: SQUINT YOUR EYES

scenes.text: And don't forget the bottom, honey. Fill the space under the tree with a tree skirt, a basket, or a few wrapped boxes, so the trunk and the stand don't show. A tree with a bare plastic stand looks like it's standing in its underwear. My grandson said that once, at Thanksgiving, and the whole family has said it ever since.
scenes.caption: IN ITS UNDERWEAR

scenes.text: And when you take it all down, wind each ribbon around a paper towel tube, and keep the topper in its own box, wrapped in tissue. Next year, you'll be finished in half the time. And the ribbon will come out smooth and ready, not crushed and wrinkled in the bottom of a box.
scenes.query: ribbon wound on paper towel tube
scenes.caption: HALF THE TIME

scenes.text: So one more time. Ribbon falling down the tree, not wrapped round. Wide and wired. One or two kinds. The ribbon before the ornaments. A topper a tenth the height of the tree. Fill in the top so it sits in a nest. And a wooden spoon tied to the trunk to hold it straight. That's how my mother and I finally made our little tree look like the window at Halle's.
scenes.caption: LIKE THE WINDOW AT HALLE'S

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. What's on top of your tree? A star, an angel, or something else? The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: STAR OR ANGEL?
